title: Sixty-Seven Garments in a Rented Flat: How Goonj Began
dek: Around 1999 a Delhi communications manager left his job to treat clothing as a matter of dignity, starting with the clothes in his own family's cupboards.

story.event: Leaving a corporate job to collect surplus city clothing for villages, starting with 67 garments
story.summary: After meeting a Delhi man who collected unclaimed bodies and whose small daughter slept beside them for warmth, and after seeing earthquake survivors in Uttarkashi refuse clothing thrown from trucks in 1991, Anshu Gupta left his job at Escorts (in 1998 by his account, 1999 by most others) and founded Goonj with his wife Meenakshi. They began with 67 garments in their rented flat in Sarita Vihar, funded from his provident fund. Goonj later paid villagers in clothing for community work under its Cloth for Work scheme, and by 2015 worked in 21 Indian states.
paragraphs: In the early 1990s Anshu Gupta, then a young freelance journalist, spent a week in Delhi following Habib, a man who lived on the pavement outside LNJP Hospital and carried unclaimed bodies to the police. He was paid 20 rupees and some cloth for each, Reader's Digest India later reported, and winter was his busy season. Habib's six-year-old daughter told Gupta that on the coldest nights she slept hugging the corpses for warmth. Gupta has said the encounter "jolted" him: in a Delhi winter, he concluded, people died less of cold than of having too little to wear.

He had seen something else in 1991, when as a student he went to Uttarkashi to help after an earthquake: villagers, he said, rejecting bundles of clothing thrown down to them from trucks. After studying mass communication and economics, he spent 1992 to 1998 in corporate jobs, the last in communications at Escorts.

Then he left. By his own account to InsideIIM he quit in 1998; Goonj and most other accounts date its start to 1999. He had no institutional money, only a small sum from his own provident fund, according to Gulf News. The first stock was 67 garments from his and his wife Meenakshi's wardrobes and from relatives, some unworn for years, and the first premises were their two-bedroom rented flat in Sarita Vihar, south Delhi. Meenakshi stayed at the BBC until 2005. People were at first hard to persuade; Gupta recalled that "it was tough explaining the concept."

What grew from the flat kept the Uttarkashi lesson at its centre: how something is given matters as much as what is given. Handouts, Gupta told Gulf News, strip people of self-respect. Under Goonj's Cloth for Work scheme, villagers choose work their community needs, such as repairing a road, digging a well or building a bamboo bridge, and are paid for their labour in clothes and other goods. When Gupta received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2015, Goonj was working in 21 of India's states and had turned scrap cloth into more than three million sanitary pads.

quote.text: You cannot help feeling that they are costly to you, and they must see that you find them a burthen? This is a perilous state of affairs, in which hatred and bitterness have every prospect of increasing
quote.locator: Book II, chapter VII (Socrates advises Aristarchus)
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates, through Xenophon, notices what dependence does to both sides: the giver feels the cost, the receiver feels a burden, and resentment grows. Cloth for Work answers the same problem from the other direction, turning a handout into an exchange in which each side brings something.

reflection: Gupta's starting stock was what was already in the cupboard. What made it more than a clothes drive was a question he kept asking about the people on the receiving end: what does this feel like from where they stand? The villagers at Uttarkashi had answered it by refusing.

You give a great deal in a week, at work and at home, often to people who are tired or worried. It is worth noticing, now and then, how your help arrives as well as whether it arrives. The same favour can leave someone feeling looked after or feeling small, and the difference is usually in the manner, not the cost.
invitation: Think of one thing you regularly do for someone, at home or at work. Today, ask them one plain question about how it could be done in a way that suits them better.

research_notes: Founding year: Gupta told InsideIIM he left his corporate career in 1998 and founded Goonj then (INK Talks also says 1998); the Magsaysay Foundation, Goonj's own site, Gupta's website, the Indian Express, Reader's Digest and Gulf News give 1999. The story gives both and uses 1999 as the date. Habib's daughter's words appear in three versions (Magsaysay: 'When I feel cold, I hug a dead body and sleep'; InsideIIM: 'When I feel cold during the night, I hug the dead body and sleep'; Reader's Digest: 'When it gets too cold, I go to sleep hugging dead bodies'), so the story paraphrases rather than quotes her. When he met Habib: Reader's Digest says the early 1990s as a freelance journalist; Gulf News quotes him as a mass communication student; InsideIIM as part of his freelance work; the story says the early 1990s. Habib's pay (Rs 20 and some cloth) comes from Reader's Digest only and is attributed. Gupta's website says Habib collected bodies 'in exchange for cloth'. Uttarkashi: Gulf News has villagers rejecting clothing thrown from trucks, Reader's Digest an old man who wanted only clothing; the story uses Gupta's own account in Gulf News. Scale figures disagree and are mostly left out: Gulf News and the Indian Express (2015) say over 1,000 tonnes a year, the Magsaysay citation more than one million kilograms a year, Reader's Digest (2019) 'around 4,000 tons so far', and Wikipedia over 3,500 tonnes a year. The story uses only the 21 states and the three million pads from the 2015 citation. Gulf News gives the flat as rented and two-bedroom; Reader's Digest says 'their own home'. Meenakshi Gupta's BBC dates come from Goonj's governing-body page. The Business Standard interviews found in the search refused automated requests and are not cited. The Xenophon passage is Socrates' advice to Aristarchus, whose idle kinswomen he urges to work at clothmaking; it is applied by analogy.
